title: The biological basis of business management

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Scientists today are increasingly looking to apply the methods of biological research to the study of business management, and it is possible that the results will provide a new set of tools for the hard-pressed business manager. Much of the existing research into the link between genes and behaviour is based on observational studies of twins. Human geneticists commonly carry out research into twins since, unlike their colleagues who study other species such as flies and mice, human geneticists are unable to breed their subjects in laboratories. The fact that identical twins share all of their DNA, and non-identical (or fraternal) twins share half, forms the basis of much research.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The consensus from the studies of twins is that genes do account for a substantial proportion of the differences between individuals — and that this applies to business as much as to the rest of life. Dr Scott Shane, professor of management at Case Western Reserve University in the USA, has found evidence of genetic influence over which jobs people choose, how satisfied they are with those jobs, how often they change jobs, how important work is to them, and how well they perform. Dr Chase even concluded that the money people make depends, at least in part, on their DNA. Around 40% of the variation between people's earnings, he says, is attributable to genes.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: However, other factors can be important too. Dr Richard Avery, of the National University of Singapore (NUS), has been studying exactly how genes interact with different types of environment to create such personal qualities as enthusiasm for business and leadership. Previous research had shown that people exhibiting traits like sensation-seeking are more likely to go into business for themselves than less outgoing people. Dr Avery found the same effect for extroversion (of which sensation-seeking was one component). There was, however, an interesting twist. His study of 1,285 pairs of identical twins, and 849 pairs of same-sex fraternal twins, suggests that genes help explain extroversion only in women. In men, the extroversion characteristic is a result of their environment. In a second twin study, this time just on men, Dr Avery investigated to what extent successful business leaders are born, and to what extent they are made. He discovered that genetic leadership traits certainly exist, but the way people are raised matters too. The influence of genes on leadership success is weakest in boys brought up with money — that is, in men from rich, supportive families — and strongest in those raised in less fortunate circumstances.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Twin studies such as these are useful, but they provide only partial explanations of what is going on. To get to the bottom of the relevant questions, it is necessary to look at molecular biology. It is generally acknowledged that one way genes affect behavior is through neurotransmitters, the chemicals in the body which carry messages between nerve cells. Two of the most important of these chemicals are dopamine (which controls feelings of pleasure and reward) and serotonin (which regulates mood). Some aspects of a person's character have been shown to depend on the amounts of certain neurotransmitters in the body. However, until recently there has been little research into their effects on attitudes to work.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Dr Song Zhaoli, also at the NUS, has gathered and analysed DNA from 123 subjects to see if a person's genetic make-up can be matched with work-related variables like job satisfaction. Dr Song told the subjects to report moments of negative mood (anger, guilt sadness or worry) and job satisfaction (measured on a seven-point scale) four times a day for a week. He compared the DNA of his volunteers with their reported moods and job satisfaction, and found that those subjects who carried a particular variant of a gene linked to the presence of the neurotransmitter serotonin were less likely to indicate negativity in their mood. What is more, he discovered that these optimists tended to report higher levels of job satisfaction.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Neurotransmitters are not the only way an individual's genetic composition affects attitudes. Hormones (which are also body chemicals) play a part. For example, the hormone cortisol has been shown to affect a person's assessment of time in relation to money. That, at least, was the conclusion of a study by Dr Taiki Takahashi of Hokkaido University in Japan. After taking saliva samples for chemical analysis from 18 volunteers, Dr Takahashi asked his subjects what the minimum amount of money was that they would want in a year's time, in return for giving up an on-the-spot payment that was equivalent to $90. He found that those with a lower base level of cortisol tended to prefer instant payment, even when the promised future compensation was much greater than $90. Then there is the principal male sex hormone, testosterone. High levels of testosterone have been correlated with risk tolerance, creativity and the willingness to go into new business ventures. In an often-cited study, Gad Saad and John Vongas of Concordia University in Canada, reported that male subjects showed a rise in their testosterone levels when their own perception of their status rose. The researchers concluded that a better understanding of the effects of testosterone could help, for example, explain why certain advertising works. It could also be useful in understanding what makes some people good in the field of sales, or other competitive areas of business.
